master.title: Daily headlines from Japan
master.content:
G7 ministers confirm close unity to preserve international order

The foreign ministers of the G7 wrapped up their three-day talks in Karuizawa, Nagano Prefecture, on Tuesday with a joint statement stating their strong opposition to any unilateral attempts to change the status quo by force and determination to preserve a free and open rules-based international order. In addition to demanding an unconditional withdrawal of Russian forces from Ukraine, the ministers also noted the importance of directly expressing concerns to China through frank discussions. On nuclear disarmament, they welcomed Japan's 'Hiroshima Action Plan' as a pragmatic approach toward realising a world without nuclear weapons. (Asahi, Yomiuri, Mainichi, Sankei, Tokyo Shimbun, Nikkei)

G7 digital ministers to adopt action plan for 'responsible AI'

The G7 ministers in charge of digital and technology policy are poised to adopt an action plan to secure a responsible environment surrounding artificial intelligence when they meet in Takasaki, Gunma Prefecture later this month, media reported. According to the report, the G7 members want to confirm their cooperation toward setting out an environment where generative AI technology such as ChatGPT can be used safely. The ministers will also reportedly agree to work together to improve trust in the internet, such as by clamping down on fake news and disinformation. (Yomiuri)

Kishida attack suspect may have been dissatisfied with politicians

The 24-year-old man arrested for throwing an explosive device at PM Fumio Kishida last Saturday had filed a lawsuit against the state last year, taking issue with electoral laws that require candidates to be at least 30 years old and be able to post a bond of 3 million JPY (20,408 EUR), media reported. Reports also said that in documents presented in connection with the lawsuit, the suspect, Ryuji Kimura, also criticised Kishida's government for deciding to organise a state funeral for slain former PM Shinzo Abe without involving the Diet, saying it was 'a challenge to democracy'. (Asahi, Yomiuri, Mainichi, Sankei)

No Japanese cars make the cut for US EV tax breaks

Some Japanese dailies reported on their front pages the news that only car models manufactured by US automakers made the US government list of electric vehicles eligible for tax credits under the Inflation Reduction Act that was released on Monday. Nissan Motor Co.'s Leaf had been on the list prior to the revision. While Tokyo and Washington agreed on rules under which Japanese models would qualify for the tax credits, observers said it would take time for Japanese automakers to meet or prove that they meet the IRA's conditions on battery components and minerals. (Tokyo Shimbun, Nikkei)

Justice ministry panel agrees to debate introduction of joint custody

An advisory panel under the Justice Ministry agreed Tuesday to discuss the issue of introducing a joint custody system for divorced parents, media reported. It marks a step toward the concept's realisation, after the body compiled an interim report last November where it mentioned the option but only in parallel with maintaining the current rules where only one parent gets custody after divorce. During Tuesday's closed-door meeting, members reportedly agreed that the introduction of joint custody should be the direction in which their discussions should proceed. Opponents to joint custody fear that this would be detrimental in cases where domestic violence had played a role in the breakdown of the marriage, but proponents argue that times - and the concept of parenting - have changed since sole custody was introduced into the Civil Code in 1947. (Asahi, Mainichi, Nikkei)

English-language papers:

Environment groups sue EU over gas, nuclear green label (The Japan News, 1/6 page w/photo)

Europe carbon footprint project for batteries highlights transparency challenges (The Japan News, 1/12 page)

Prepared based on the vernacular press by Mari Koseki

Chief Press Officer, Political, Press and Information Section, EU Delegation to Japan
